/-!
# Earth–Moon problem

The Earth–Moon problem, posed by Gerhard Ringel in 1959, asks for the maximum chromatic number
of a biplanar graph, i.e. of a finite simple graph whose edges can be partitioned into two
planar subgraphs (a graph of thickness at most two). It is known that this maximum is at least
$9$ (Sulanke, 1974: the join $K_6 + C_5$ needs $9$ colours) and at most $12$ (Ringel, 1959).
Ringel conjectured the answer $8$, which Sulanke's example refuted; Gethner conjectured in 2018
that the answer is $11$.

Mathlib has no notion of planar graph, so this file defines planarity directly: a graph is
planar if it has a drawing in the Euclidean plane with vertices as distinct points and edges as
simple arcs that meet only at common endpoints.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Earth–Moon problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%E2%80%93Moon_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Open Problem Garden, Earth-Moon Problem](http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/earth_moon_problem)
- [Ri59] Ringel, G., *Färbungsprobleme auf Flächen und Graphen*, VEB Deutscher Verlag der
  Wissenschaften, Berlin (1959).
- [Ge18] Gethner, E., *To the Moon and beyond*, in: Graph Theory: Favorite Conjectures and
  Open Problems, II, Springer (2018), 115–133.
  [doi:10.1007/978-3-319-97686-0_11](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-97686-0_11)
-/

blocks.docstring:
A **planar drawing** of a simple graph `G`. The vertices are placed at distinct points of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. Every edge `e` is drawn as a simple arc `arc e`, a continuous
injective map from $[0,1]$ into $\mathbb{R}^2$, whose two end points are the points of the two
end vertices of `e`. An arc passes through a vertex point only at its end points, and two distinct
arcs meet only in vertex points (hence only in common end vertices).

justification.closest_existing_considered: SimpleGraph.UnitDistancePlaneGraph / UnitDistanceEmbeddable (FormalConjecturesForMathlib) only place vertices in ℝ^n with unit-length edges, and say nothing about edge crossings; Mathlib's `Path`/`ContinuousMap`/`unitInterval` are used as building blocks. Searched Mathlib and the repo for planar, Kuratowski, Wagner, thickness, minor, subdivision: nothing.
justification.name: EarthMoonProblem.PlanarDrawing
justification.why_needed: Neither Mathlib nor FormalConjecturesForMathlib defines planar graphs (nor graph minors/subdivisions that a Kuratowski/Wagner criterion would need). A structure packaging a planar embedding: injective vertex placement in ℝ², a simple arc C(unitInterval, ℝ²) per edge joining the images of its endpoints, arcs avoiding vertex points except at their endpoints, and distinct arcs meeting only in vertex points.

blocks.name: IsBiplanar
blocks.text:
/-- A simple graph is **biplanar** (has thickness at most two) if its edge set can be partitioned
into two subsets such that the two corresponding spanning subgraphs are both planar. -/
def IsBiplanar (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ G₁ G₂ : SimpleGraph V,
    Disjoint G₁ G₂ ∧ G₁ ⊔ G₂ = G ∧ IsPlanar G₁ ∧ IsPlanar G₂

@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem isPlanar_bot_of_injective (f : V → ℝ²) (hf : Function.Injective f) :
    IsPlanar (⊥ : SimpleGraph V) :=
  have : IsEmpty (⊥ : SimpleGraph V).edgeSet := by simp
  ⟨{ vertex := f
     vertex_injective := hf
     arc := isEmptyElim
     arc_injective := isEmptyElim
     arc_ends := isEmptyElim
     arc_vertex := isEmptyElim
     arc_inter := isEmptyElim }⟩

@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem isPlanar_top_fin_two : IsPlanar (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)) := by
  have hEq : ∀ e ∈ (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)).edgeSet, e = s(0, 1) := by
    intro e he
    induction e with | h a b =>
    simp only [mem_edgeSet, top_adj] at he
    fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp_all [Sym2.eq_swap]
  let p : Fin 2 → ℝ² := fun i => EuclideanSpace.single 0 (i : ℝ)
  have hp : p 0 ≠ p 1 := by
    intro h
    have := congrArg (fun x : ℝ² => x 0) h
    simp [p] at this
  have hline : Function.Injective (AffineMap.lineMap (p 0) (p 1) : ℝ → ℝ²) :=
    AffineMap.lineMap_injective ℝ hp
  exact ⟨{ vertex := p
           vertex_injective := fun a b h => by
             fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp_all
           arc := fun _ => ⟨fun t => AffineMap.lineMap (p 0) (p 1) (t : ℝ), by fun_prop⟩
           arc_injective := fun e s t hst => Subtype.ext (hline hst)
           arc_ends := fun e => by
             have := hEq e e.2
             simp [this]
           arc_vertex := fun e t ⟨w, hw⟩ => by
             fin_cases w
             · left
               refine Subtype.ext (hline ?_)
               simpa using hw.symm
             · right
               refine Subtype.ext (hline ?_)
               simpa using hw.symm
           arc_inter := fun e₁ e₂ h =>
             (h (Subtype.ext ((hEq _ e₁.2).trans (hEq _ e₂.2).symm))).elim }⟩

claims.decomposer_note: Single open-ended question whose Prop is 'sup of χ(G) over all finite simple biplanar graphs G (edge set partitionable into two planar subgraphs, i.e. thickness ≤ 2) equals c' with c = answer(sorry) in repo idiom (cf. ErdosProblems/508.lean); the background asserts candidate answers — Gethner's 2018 conjecture c = 11 (Ringel's original c = 8 was refuted by Sulanke's K₆ + C₅), with 9 ≤ c ≤ 12 known so the maximum exists — and since Mathlib/FormalConjecturesForMathlib have no planar-graph or thickness definition, biplanarity must be defined (e.g. via a planarity criterion such as Kuratowski/Wagner) restricted to finite simple graphs.
claims.reviewer_why: c01's declaration `IsGreatest {χ : ℕ | ∃ n (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), IsBiplanar G ∧ G.chromaticNumber = χ} answer(sorry)` faithfully encodes 'the maximum chromatic number of (finite simple) biplanar graphs': the set is exactly the chromatic numbers of finite biplanar graphs (finite graphs have finite χ; n = 0 only adds 0 harmlessly), the maximum exists (Ringel's bound 12), and IsGreatest uniquely constrains the ℕ-valued answer. `IsBiplanar` is a literal edge partition into two planar spanning subgraphs (thickness ≤ 2; isolated vertices irrelevant). `IsPlanar` uses the primary topological definition (injective vertex placement in ℝ², edges as injective continuous arcs on [0,1] with the right endpoints, arcs hit vertex points only at t = 0, 1, distinct arcs meet only in vertex points) which I checked reproduces the standard Diestel definition; it does not rely on Wagner's theorem as c03–c08 do (those are also faithful for finite graphs, but a definition-by-theorem). c02 is equivalent but more verbose. sSup-in-ℕ∞ variants (c03, c06–c08) are equivalent given the known bound but encode 'maximum' less directly and have thinner documentation. Edits: added a proven test `isPlanar_top_fin_two` (adapted from c02) showing a single edge has a PlanarDrawing, and removed the un-adjudicated sorry'd variants (upper/lower bound, Gethner).

context:
The Earth–Moon problem is an unsolved problem on graph coloring in mathematics. It is an extension of the planar map coloring problem (solved by the four color theorem), and was posed by Gerhard Ringel in 1959. An intuitive form of the problem asks how many colors are needed to color political maps of the Earth and Moon, in a hypothetical future where each Earth country has a Moon colony which must be given the same color. In mathematical terms, it seeks the chromatic number of biplanar graphs. It is known that this number is at least 9 and at most 12.
The Earth–Moon problem has been extended to analogous problems of coloring maps on any number of planets. For this extension the lower bounds and upper bounds on the number of colors are closer, within two of each other. One real-world application of the Earth–Moon problem involves testing printed circuit boards.

decomposition_objections.text: None. The single-slot table is correct: the list entry is one open-ended question, and the article confirms the precise reading 'maximum chromatic number of biplanar graphs (thickness ≤ 2)'. I followed the note's guidance to define biplanarity myself, but chose the topological (drawing) definition of planarity over a Kuratowski/Wagner criterion, since using a criterion as the definition would make faithfulness depend on a deep theorem.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Earth–Moon problem

The Earth–Moon problem, posed by Gerhard Ringel in 1959, asks for the maximum chromatic number
of a biplanar graph, i.e. of a finite simple graph whose edges can be partitioned into two
planar subgraphs (a graph of thickness at most two). It is known that this maximum is at least
$9$ (Sulanke, 1974: the join $K_6 + C_5$ needs $9$ colours) and at most $12$ (Ringel, 1959).
Ringel conjectured the answer $8$, which Sulanke's example refuted; Gethner conjectured in 2018
that the answer is $11$.

Mathlib has no notion of planar graph, so this file defines planarity directly: a graph is
planar if it has a drawing in the Euclidean plane with vertices as distinct points and edges as
simple arcs that meet only at common endpoints.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Earth–Moon problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%E2%80%93Moon_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Open Problem Garden, Earth-Moon Problem](http://www.openproblemgarden.org/op/earth_moon_problem)
- [Ri59] Ringel, G., *Färbungsprobleme auf Flächen und Graphen*, VEB Deutscher Verlag der
  Wissenschaften, Berlin (1959).
- [Ge18] Gethner, E., *To the Moon and beyond*, in: Graph Theory: Favorite Conjectures and
  Open Problems, II, Springer (2018), 115–133.
  [doi:10.1007/978-3-319-97686-0_11](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-97686-0_11)
-/

open SimpleGraph
open scoped EuclideanGeometry unitInterval

namespace EarthMoonProblem

variable {V : Type*}

/-- A **planar drawing** of a simple graph `G`. The vertices are placed at distinct points of the
Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. Every edge `e` is drawn as a simple arc `arc e`, a continuous
injective map from $[0,1]$ into $\mathbb{R}^2$, whose two end points are the points of the two
end vertices of `e`. An arc passes through a vertex point only at its end points, and two distinct
arcs meet only in vertex points (hence only in common end vertices). -/
structure PlanarDrawing (G : SimpleGraph V) where
  /-- The point of the plane at which a vertex is drawn. -/
  vertex : V → ℝ²
  vertex_injective : Function.Injective vertex
  /-- The simple arc along which an edge is drawn. -/
  arc : G.edgeSet → C(I, ℝ²)
  arc_injective : ∀ e, Function.Injective (arc e)
  /-- The end points of the arc of `e` are the points of the two end vertices of `e`. -/
  arc_ends : ∀ e : G.edgeSet, s(arc e 0, arc e 1) = (e : Sym2 V).map vertex
  /-- An arc meets a vertex point only at its own end points. -/
  arc_vertex : ∀ (e : G.edgeSet) (t : I), arc e t ∈ Set.range vertex → t = 0 ∨ t = 1
  /-- Two distinct arcs meet only in vertex points. -/
  arc_inter : ∀ e e' : G.edgeSet, e ≠ e' →
    Set.range (arc e) ∩ Set.range (arc e') ⊆ Set.range vertex

/-- A simple graph is **planar** if it has a planar drawing. -/
def IsPlanar (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  Nonempty (PlanarDrawing G)

/-- A simple graph is **biplanar** (has thickness at most two) if its edge set can be partitioned
into two subsets such that the two corresponding spanning subgraphs are both planar. -/
def IsBiplanar (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ G₁ G₂ : SimpleGraph V,
    Disjoint G₁ G₂ ∧ G₁ ⊔ G₂ = G ∧ IsPlanar G₁ ∧ IsPlanar G₂

/-- If the vertex type injects into the plane, the empty graph on it is planar: place the
vertices at the given points and draw no arcs. -/
@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem isPlanar_bot_of_injective (f : V → ℝ²) (hf : Function.Injective f) :
    IsPlanar (⊥ : SimpleGraph V) :=
  have : IsEmpty (⊥ : SimpleGraph V).edgeSet := by simp
  ⟨{ vertex := f
     vertex_injective := hf
     arc := isEmptyElim
     arc_injective := isEmptyElim
     arc_ends := isEmptyElim
     arc_vertex := isEmptyElim
     arc_inter := isEmptyElim }⟩

/-- Every planar graph is biplanar. -/
@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem IsPlanar.isBiplanar {G : SimpleGraph V} (hG : IsPlanar G) : IsBiplanar G :=
  have ⟨D⟩ := hG
  ⟨G, ⊥, disjoint_bot_right, sup_bot_eq G, hG,
    isPlanar_bot_of_injective D.vertex D.vertex_injective⟩

/-- The empty graph on finitely many vertices is planar. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem isPlanar_bot (n : ℕ) : IsPlanar (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) :=
  isPlanar_bot_of_injective (fun i => !₂[(i : ℝ), 0]) fun i j h =>
    Fin.ext <| Nat.cast_injective (R := ℝ) <| by simpa [PiLp.ext_iff, Fin.forall_fin_two] using h

/-- The graph with a single edge is planar: draw the edge as a straight segment. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem isPlanar_top_fin_two : IsPlanar (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)) := by
  have hEq : ∀ e ∈ (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)).edgeSet, e = s(0, 1) := by
    intro e he
    induction e with | h a b =>
    simp only [mem_edgeSet, top_adj] at he
    fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp_all [Sym2.eq_swap]
  let p : Fin 2 → ℝ² := fun i => EuclideanSpace.single 0 (i : ℝ)
  have hp : p 0 ≠ p 1 := by
    intro h
    have := congrArg (fun x : ℝ² => x 0) h
    simp [p] at this
  have hline : Function.Injective (AffineMap.lineMap (p 0) (p 1) : ℝ → ℝ²) :=
    AffineMap.lineMap_injective ℝ hp
  exact ⟨{ vertex := p
           vertex_injective := fun a b h => by
             fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp_all
           arc := fun _ => ⟨fun t => AffineMap.lineMap (p 0) (p 1) (t : ℝ), by fun_prop⟩
           arc_injective := fun e s t hst => Subtype.ext (hline hst)
           arc_ends := fun e => by
             have := hEq e e.2
             simp [this]
           arc_vertex := fun e t ⟨w, hw⟩ => by
             fin_cases w
             · left
               refine Subtype.ext (hline ?_)
               simpa using hw.symm
             · right
               refine Subtype.ext (hline ?_)
               simpa using hw.symm
           arc_inter := fun e₁ e₂ h =>
             (h (Subtype.ext ((hEq _ e₁.2).trans (hEq _ e₂.2).symm))).elim }⟩

/-- **The Earth–Moon problem** (Ringel, 1959): what is the maximum chromatic number of biplanar
graphs? That is, determine the greatest value of the chromatic number $\chi(G)$ over all finite
simple biplanar graphs $G$. It is known that this maximum lies between $9$ and $12$, and
Gethner conjectures that it is $11$. -/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem earth_moon_problem :
    IsGreatest
      {χ : ℕ | ∃ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), IsBiplanar G ∧ G.chromaticNumber = χ}
      answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

end EarthMoonProblem

items: Planarity is defined topologically (the primary definition), not via a Kuratowski/Wagner criterion: a `PlanarDrawing` of G consists of an injective map vertex : V → ℝ² (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)), and for each edge e a continuous injective arc arc e : C(unitInterval, ℝ²) with s(arc e 0, arc e 1) = e.map vertex, such that an arc meets a vertex point only at t = 0 or t = 1, and two distinct arcs meet only in vertex points (hence, combined with the previous condition, only at common end vertices). `IsPlanar G := Nonempty (PlanarDrawing G)`. Reviewers should check these four conditions capture 'edges intersect only at common endpoints'.

Arcs are required to be injective (simple/Jordan arcs), matching the standard definition of a planar embedding; for finite graphs this is equivalent to allowing arbitrary continuous curves with the same disjointness conditions.

`IsBiplanar G := ∃ G₁ G₂, Disjoint G₁ G₂ ∧ G₁ ⊔ G₂ = G ∧ IsPlanar G₁ ∧ IsPlanar G₂`, i.e. literally a partition of the edge set into two planar spanning subgraphs (thickness ≤ 2). Planar graphs are therefore biplanar (one part may be empty); this matches the article's 'edges can be partitioned into two subsets such that the corresponding two subgraphs are both planar' and does not affect the maximum chromatic number. Disjointness is included for literal faithfulness; dropping it would be equivalent since subgraphs of planar graphs are planar.

Finite simple graphs are quantified as `SimpleGraph (Fin n)` for all n : ℕ (repo idiom, cf. ErdosProblems/1104.lean); chromatic number and biplanarity are isomorphism invariants, so this loses no generality. The case n = 0 contributes χ = 0 harmlessly.

The set of chromatic numbers is taken in ℕ (with `G.chromaticNumber = ↑χ` in ℕ∞), since finite graphs have finite chromatic number; the answer is thus a natural number. `IsGreatest` (rather than `sSup`) is used because the article's 'maximum' exists (9 ≤ max ≤ 12) and IsGreatest also asserts that some biplanar graph attains it, avoiding ℕ's `sSup ∅ = 0` / unbounded-set defaults.
'Biplanar' is read as thickness ≤ 2 (edge set partitionable into two planar subgraphs) rather than thickness exactly 2; the two readings give the same maximum since every planar graph has χ ≤ 4 < 9.

Extra declarations beyond the slot: `earth_moon_problem.variants.upper_bound` (χ ≤ 12 for biplanar graphs, Ringel 1959, research solved), `earth_moon_problem.variants.lower_bound` (∃ biplanar G with 9 ≤ χ(G), Sulanke 1974, research solved; stated existentially because Mathlib has no graph-join operation to write K₆ + C₅ directly), `earth_moon_problem.variants.gethner` (Gethner's 2018 conjecture that the maximum is 11, research open), plus two proven API lemmas (`isPlanar_bot_of_injective`, `IsPlanar.isBiplanar`) and one proven test (`isPlanar_bot`) for the bespoke definitions.

The bespoke definitions live in the problem namespace `EarthMoonProblem` (as `PlanarDrawing G`, `IsPlanar G`, `IsBiplanar G`) rather than in FormalConjecturesForMathlib, since the task restricts output to a single problem file; they are generic enough that a maintainer might prefer moving them to FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/.

reviewer_notes: The list entry is terse; the article fixes the reading: max χ over finite simple graphs of thickness ≤ 2, known to lie in [9, 12], so the maximum exists and `IsGreatest` with `answer(sorry) : ℕ` is well-posed. Thickness ≤ 2 vs exactly 2 is immaterial for the maximum (planar graphs have χ ≤ 4). No candidate omitted the slot; all compile.
